Every day is a little adventure

03 · Two ways to play

Choose at New Game

Histoire · Story

  • 62 quests in four lanes, each opening the next
  • Four great deeds, then the descent into the Heart
  • A painted page in the My Story book for every quest
  • Ends with a lullaby and the credits; the world carries on

Survie · Survival

  • The endless game: score = hours survived
  • Rewards unlock with days and milestones instead of quests
  • Nights grow harder, up to 14 attackers
  • A lost day after a collapse never counts

Both modes: same world, gentle mode for young players, maths level 1–6 changeable at any time.

06 · Fight and build

Real action, real walls

Action combat

  • Attack button, combo swings, run and dodge, knockback
  • Blade, blunt and pierce: every monster has a weakness
  • 7 weapons, stone and shell armour, 5 outfits
  • 29 monsters including 4 bosses
  • Gentle mode halves all damage

  • Stone, wood, brick, obsidian and snow blocks
  • Web or metal binding lets rows overhang
  • Ladders, gates, spikes, web traps; build mode on keyboard and pad

Play

Open the file and go

No install and no account. The game runs in Chrome on a computer or a phone held sideways.

  1. Open mine-moule.html

    Download it from the repository and open it in your browser. On a phone, turn it sideways.

  2. Start a New Game

    Pick a name, a world, a season length, Story or Survival, and a maths level from 1 to 6.

  3. Build the bed first

    Grandma’s three-picture prologue sets the scene. Gather wood and webs, craft at the workbench, and be inside before the first night. The line under the map always shows the quest you are on.

  4. Keep your save safe

    Saves live in the browser. Export one from the pause menu; import it from the title screen.

What is in 1.11

Features

Survive

Days, nights and seasons

  • Day–night clock and four seasons with weather
  • Energy and hunger, 6 cooked dishes and a hunt with real animations
  • Night sieges when you are home, Grandma’s garden, village guards
  • Fishing all year (through the ice in winter), villages to trade with

Fight

Action combat

  • Six sword swings and three hammer swings, chained at random
  • Run and dodge with a double tap; a rock thrower that aims itself
  • 7 weapons with blade, blunt and pierce; stone and shell armour, 5 outfits
  • 29 monsters, 4 bosses with their own attacks

Build

Building in the wild

  • Stone, wood, brick, obsidian, snow
  • Web and metal binding for bridges and roofs
  • Build mode on keyboard and gamepad
  • Tent, campfire and field bench you set down and pack up anywhere

Explore

Six lands

  • Homelands, Far Shore, Frozen North, Badlands, Sky Islands
  • Grandma’s painted map or a Metro map, with zoom and quick travel
  • Caves with secret rooms, climbing walls, cliffs and ravines at the edges
  • Lantern, silver lantern and a headlamp that lights the night

Story

62 quests

  • Four lanes, four great deeds, one finale
  • A journal with full tasks, rewards and lock hints; the quest you are on stays on screen
  • Notice boards, villagers with their own voice, Grandma’s prologue

Learn

For young players

  • Maths questions at levels 1 to 6, picked on a lock wheel

Design

The decisions behind the game

The main choices we made, grouped by topic, each with the reason behind it.

Goal and modes

  • Two modes at New Game

    Story has 62 quests and an ending; Survival is endless and scored in hours survived.

    Why One game for children who want a story and players who want a challenge.

  • Season length 7, 14 or 28 days

    Chosen at New Game; seasons change palettes, weather, food and the length of nights.

    Why Short seasons for quick games, long ones for slow builders.

  • French first, English anytime

    Every text exists in both languages; the flags switch instantly.

    Why It was made in a French-speaking home.

World

  • Generated from a seed

    Each save gets its own world: three flavours (Valley, Cove, Hills) weight the terrain types.

    Why Every new game is a new map to explore.

  • Six lands opened by the story

    The troll’s ravine leads to the Far Shore, an iron key to the North, the Frost King to the fork, four great deeds to the Heart.

    Why Progress you can see on the map.

  • Danger rings

    Monsters get tougher with distance from home and with the weeks, capped at +25 %. The far lands start at 1.6× and climb to 2.25×; bosses keep their own health.

    Why Home stays safe enough; adventure stays exciting.

  • Every world can be finished

    Generation guarantees what the story needs: two caves with a music-box room and a dragon room, the brigand camp, the sunken library, shield crabs, a thief crow and enough monsters for every kill quest.

    Why A child should never be stuck on a quest that cannot exist. A 256-world census checks it.

  • Nature closes the world

    Each region ends at a cliff, a bottomless ravine or a bramble wall, drawn for its land.

    Why A wall of bricks broke the spell.

Survival and home

  • Two needs: energy and hunger

    Energy empties in 2.5 days, hunger fills in 2. Food, sleep and shelter refill them.

    Why Simple enough for a child to plan around.

  • Waking up, not game over

    At zero energy you wake in your bed or shelter; in Survival that day does not count.

    Why Failure costs time, never the whole game.

  • Night sieges

    2 + day ÷ 2 attackers, up to 14 (10 during the Great Siege), only on nights you are home. Monsters still standing at dawn trample Grandma’s garden. Two guards help after “The Leaky Roof”.

    Why A reason to come home, without punishing long trips.

  • Villages trade or remember

    Steal freely or trade; six thefts anger a village for a season.

    Why Choices with consequences, but forgivable.

  • Quick travel costs the trip

    Any place you have found on the map is one click away, but you pay the time, energy and hunger of running there. You may arrive tired, never dead.

    Why Saves the walk without making the world small.

  • Falls measured from take-off

    Only drops of more than 1.5× the highest jump (about 4½ blocks) below where you jumped hurt.

    Why Jumping off your own tower should be fun.

  • Camp gear you keep

    The tent, campfire and field bench are tools: set them down, use them, pack them up. A night in the tent restores you fully.

    Why Little houses far from home.

Combat

  • Full action combat

    An attack button replaces the old automatic exchange. Monsters wind up before they strike; hits knock back and give a moment of safety.

    Why Skill and timing matter; fights feel fair.

  • Blade, blunt and pierce

    Each weapon has a type, each monster a weakness worth 1.5× and armour against the rest.

    Why The bestiary becomes useful, not just a collection.

  • Gentle mode

    Halves every kind of damage, including the climates.

    Why Young players can still finish the story.

Building

  • Real but simple physics

    Blocks on a 32 px grid, up to 8 high, standing while their weight sits over a support.

    Why Easy to understand, satisfying to get right.

  • Web and metal binding

    A bound row can overhang: wood 3, stone 2, brick 4, obsidian 3, one more with metal. Web burns, so lava bridges need metal.

    Why Bridges and roofs become puzzles.

  • Shelters count as beds

    Roofed walls keep out the cold, give a respawn point and stop monsters spawning inside.

    Why Building in the wild has a purpose.

  • Spiders climb three blocks

    They try, fail and fall on taller walls. No arrow slits: walls are walls.

    Why A clear rule players can beat.

Story and learning

  • Quests are data

    The game only sends events (crafted, killed, delivered, reached); one table holds all 62 quests.

    Why Easy to add, test and balance.

  • Someone gives every quest

    Village boards, “!” villagers with their own opening lines, Grandma’s notes in the journal, the troll and the elders. Every quest shows its reward, and locked pages say what opens them.

    Why The world explains itself.

  • Maths at the player’s level

    Scholar’s stones ask grade 1–6 questions, read aloud on request; gate stones are a little harder.

    Why Practice that unlocks something real.

  • A book that writes itself

    My Story adds a painted half-page with a drop capital for every finished quest.

    Why Children see their own story grow.

  • Nothing is lost by doing it early

    Breaking the arcade wall, finding a secret room or crafting an item before its quest opens still counts when the quest does.

    Why Curious players should be rewarded, not punished.

  • The quest you are on stays on screen

    A line under the map names the current quest and its progress; Enter in the journal picks another.

    Why The first minute and every return to the game should be clear.

Look and sound

  • 960 × 540, whole-number scaling

    32 px blocks, a hero two blocks tall, crisp on laptops and phones.

    Why Modern screens, classic pixels.

  • All art drawn by code

    Three-tone shading, 2 px outlines, dithered skies, parallax and warm night lights; monsters from sprite maps.

    Why One file, no image assets, easy to recolour.

  • Readable text first

    Nunito for every word and number, the pixel font only for the logo.

    Why The maths stones must be easy to read.

  • Twenty songs, four moods

    The Kick la Banane synth engine plays each song by day and night in four seasonal arrangements; the final lullaby is the music box tune.

    Why The music is part of the story.

  • Two hand-made maps

    Grandma’s painted map and a clean Metro map, with zoom, little drawn scenes and your builds.

    Why Seeing the world grow is half the fun.

Platform

  • One HTML file, no build step

    Open it in a browser and play. Chrome on desktop and phones, touch overlay, a PlayStation-style pad for everything including the map and build mode, and full screen with P.

    Why Nothing to install, nothing to break.

  • Saves you can carry

    Three slots in browser storage, plus export to a file and import into a free slot.

    Why Phones sometimes clear storage.

  • Tested like a product

    Playwright scripts for every system and a random-input soak before each release; agent playtests across hundreds of generated worlds.

    Why A family game should not crash.

The world

Six lands, one long walk

Every world is generated from a seed and saved with its slot. Each place is two to four screens of four seconds’ walk, and every region ends at a cliff, a ravine or brambles.

Homelands

27 places · start

Forests, lakes, mountains, plains, villages with long Quebec names, cemeteries and at least two caves around the little house. At the east end, the troll guards a ravine bridge with a maths stone.

The Far Shore

33 places · rings 1–4

Wolves, wraiths, a brigand camp, the crab beach and a hamlet. Under its lake (or a market’s old well) lies the Sunken Library. An iron key opens the second crossing.

The Frozen North

12 places · cold

Fur coats, campfires and igloos keep you warm. Yetis, cursed snowmen, penguins and a grumpy walrus. The Frost King waits in the ice hall.

The Badlands

11 places · heat

A water flask, metal-bound bridges over lava, imps that burn wood and obsidian golems. The Lord of Embers guards the black forge.

The Sky Islands

10 places · wind

Wind cloaks, islands over the void, harpies and gust sprites to catch in a bottle. The Queen of Winds rules from her tower.

The Heart

5 halls · all three climates

A shaft under the house leads to the Hall of Scholars, the Hall of Climates, the Hall of the Siege and the Great Mussel.

Story mode

Grandma’s last riddle

Grandma left two things: the little house and a book of blank pages. Her notes lead through four lanes of quests to the three seals and the song that puts the Great Mussel back to sleep. A three-picture prologue opens every new story.

Le Foyer Home

Bed, chest, village boards, the pup, the leaking roof, the guards and forts. Ends with E1 · The Great Siege: hold the house three nights (not necessarily in a row); the guards leave you their banner.

Les Profondeurs The Depths

Caves, the miner, Grandma’s notes, the music box and the bestiary. Ends with E2 · The Sunken Library: seven stones under a lake or an old well as the water rises; the golden abacus.

Le Large The Far Shore and the North

The troll, coaches, the crab beach, the stubborn boar, the igloo elder and ice fishing. Ends with E3 · The Frost King and the first seal, the frost crown.

Les Climats The Lands

The water flask, lava bridges, the black forge, wind cloaks and the wind harps. Ends with E4 · Embers and Winds: two bosses, two seals.

The finale · Au cœur de la Mine-Moule

With all four deeds done, a shaft opens in the floor of the secret arcade room. Three harder scholar’s stones, a hall of cold, heat and wind, a siege with the village guards, and then the Great Mussel. She cannot be beaten by the sword: at half strength, play her the music box with the three seals, and she falls asleep. The credits roll, the Scholar costume unlocks, and the world carries on.

Reference

The numbers

Copied from the game’s data for version 1.11.2. Open a section to see it.

Monsters 29

Base health is shown; away from home it grows with the danger ring, up to +25 % from the weeks; in the far lands it starts at 1.6× and climbs to 2.25×, and bosses keep their base health. The obsidian golem never needs more than 30 hits. Weapons that match a weakness do 1.5× damage. Armour removes that share of damage unless the weapon pierces.

Time, needs and nights

A day lasts 5 minutes: 30 s of dawn, 180 s of day in summer (135 s in winter), 30 s of dusk, and the rest night. Seasons last 7, 14 or 28 days.

Energy empties in 2.5 days, faster when fighting, gathering or in a harsh climate without the right outfit. Hunger fills in 2 days. Raw food −25 %, cooked −40 %, bœuf bourguignon −100 %.

Sleep: a night in bed or in the tent restores everything. At zero energy you wake in your bed or shelter.

Fishing: all year, slower in autumn, through a hole in the ice in winter; 3 catches per spot per day. Every market sells 3 fish for 2 metal. Ore grows back each season; scholar’s stones wake a week after you solve them.

Night sieges: 2 + day ÷ 2 attackers, up to 14 (10 while the Great Siege is open), only on nights you are home. Monsters left at dawn trample the garden; replant a row for 2 wood. Two guards defend from quest F10 (Survival: day 20).

Danger rings: 0 at home to 4 at the far end of the Far Shore (up to 1.8×), plus a weekly bump capped at +25 %. The far lands start at 1.6× and climb with distance, capped at 2.25×. Falls only hurt beyond about 4½ blocks below take-off.

Build history

From a first night to the final lullaby

Each version below was playable from start to finish when it shipped. The same notes are in the game: click the version number on the title screen.

  1. 1.11.2
    • The Great Siege really caps at 10 monsters a night (a leftover setting raised it back to 14 when you were home).
  2. 1.11.1
    • Fix: a game saved before 1.11 stayed on a black screen when loaded. It loads again, and quests you had already done complete when you wake up.
  3. 1.11.0
    • Every story can now be finished: each world has the brigand camp, the sunken library (under a lake or a market’s old well), at least 2 shield crabs, a thief crow near home, two caves, a music-box room and a dragon room.
    • Mimic chests finally exist: while their quest is open, one sleeps in the first hall of every cave and wakes when you come close.
    • Nothing is lost any more: breaking the arcade wall, finding a secret room, solving the Crossing stone or crafting an item before its quest now counts when the quest opens.
    • The journal shows the whole task, its reward and what unlocks locked pages; the Finale has its own row. Enter shows a quest on screen, under the map.
    • English quest names; French and English texts now match what the game checks (L11, C4, E2, F3, F5, F9…), with no internal codes.
    • Notice boards: the chosen row opens up with the task and reward. Villagers talk in their own voice. A three-picture prologue from Grandma.
    • Fish bite all year (through the ice in winter), 3 catches per spot per day, and every market sells 3 fish for 2 metal.
    • Less grind: 6 imps, 2 crabs, 2 beetles, 2 harpies, a third gargoyle; the Great Siege caps at 10 monsters and a lost night no longer wipes the others; the tent restores full energy.
    • The Lands start at 1.6× and get harder with distance; the golem falls in 30 hits at most and says what to use; the obsidian blade pierces armour.
    • Ore grows back every season and scholar’s stones wake up a week after you solve them.
  4. 1.10.4
    • Caves keep their doorstep clear: no more boulder, stone pile or riddle stone in front of the opening.
    • A cave at the very end of a region is no longer half hidden by the cliff (or under the Frozen North arch): it moves away from the edge.
  5. 1.10.3
    • Rock thrower: it aims by itself at the closest monster within half a screen (the hero turns toward it), and the stone follows a real curve under gravity — from the top of a tower it dives onto its target. With nothing in range, it is a lob that lands about half a screen away.
    • The stone spins in flight and leaves a small trail.
  6. 1.10.2
    • Quick travel: numbers view keeps the Energy / Hunger icons and titles; only the numbers replace the bars.
    • Quick travel: as long as you arrive alive (a little energy left and not starving), the trip is allowed, even running on empty — a yellow warning tells you. It is only refused if you would collapse on the way.
  7. 1.10.1
    • Quick travel: by default the window shows your real energy and hunger bars, and the slice that will shrink or grow breathes in and out (red if the trip can’t be done). Tab (or the little switch at the top) flips to the numbers.
  8. 1.10.0
    • Quick travel from the world map: pick any place you have discovered, then “Quick travel” (Enter, ✕ on a controller, or click). The trip is instant, but it costs the time, energy and hunger of running all the way there — even through the passages between rings.
    • The confirm window shows the time, energy and hunger before → after. If you are too worn out or too hungry to last the trip, in the middle of a fight, or in a cave, the trip is refused and the reason shown.
  9. 1.9.5
    • Falls: what counts now is how far below your take-off point you land — a normal jump’s arc is free. You only get hurt beyond 1.5× the highest jump (about 4½ blocks): jumping off a 3-block tower or down one step no longer hurts.
  10. 1.9.4
    • The end of the world is no longer a brick wall: nature stops you. A sheer cliff rising past the top of the screen (icy in the Frozen North, veined with lava in the Badlands), a bottomless ravine with a broken fence and a “!” sign (lava at the bottom in the Badlands, clouds in the Sky Islands), or an impassable wall of brambles.
    • Beyond the edge everything is drawn now: no more odd trails when it rains, and the headlamp lights the cliff properly.
    • The hero says what is blocking the way: cliff, ravine or brambles.
  11. 1.9.3
    • Villages: real long Quebec-style names, with dashes and oddly specific extras — Saint-Caillou-des-Sept-Corneilles, Sainte-Pomme-de-l’Épouvante, Mont-Gravier-de-la-Dernière-Chance, Saint-Grelot-du-Ha! Ha!, Notre-Dame-du-Bon-Bouillon… Your save keeps its villages in the same places, only the names change.
    • On the map overview the start of the name is enough (Saint-Caillou…); zoom in to read the whole name. In the map panel, long names wrap onto two lines.
  12. 1.9.2
    • Headlamp: the third lantern evolution, after the silver lantern (upgraded oven: 2 gold, 1 silver, 2 metal, 1 web). It keeps everything the silver lantern does and, at night, a soft beam leaves your forehead in the direction you face and lights the path up to half the screen. It swings smoothly when you turn around and switches on by itself at dusk.
    • The field bench no longer cooks: that’s the campfire’s job. The window title now says “Field bench” or “Campfire”.
  13. 1.9.1
    • Pause menu: every tile is repainted as if by a kid with poster paint — wobbly fat lines, colours spilling over, stars and hearts: an open book under a smiling sun, a cape and crown, a treasure map (or a silly subway), notes dancing on a rainbow, a drum going BOOM, two chatting birds, a cat asleep on a pillow. Off means scribbled out in red crayon.

What comes next

Roadmap and known limits

Next

  • Costume quests: new quests that unlock hero costumes beyond the Scholar.
  • Shorter waits: the village fair (F12) still asks for about a week of patience.
  • Balance from family play: agent playtests cleared the blockers; real games will tune energy, prices and monster numbers.
  • Fonts inside the file, so the game looks the same with no internet.
  • Real-device checks on phones, tablets and a PlayStation pad.
  • Bigger saves: move to IndexedDB with compression if long games outgrow browser storage.

Known limits in 1.11

  • A siege night only counts for the Great Siege if no monster is left when you go to bed or at dawn.
  • The Heart has three halls before the Mussel; a darkness stage and a collapsing climb were left out to keep the finale short for young players.
  • The village festival and guard parades are visual only.
  • Offline, the game uses a system font instead of Nunito.
  • Exporting a save needs the game opened as a file; some hosted viewers block downloads.

How it was made

Planned first

A living plan, four brainstorm rounds and a dozen review rounds checked the story, the items and the shortcuts before any code.

Built in chapters

Combat, danger, story, the North, the two lands, the finale: each chapter ended with a recorded playthrough.

Tested every time

78 automated test scripts and a random-input soak before each release. In 1.11, agents checked 256 generated worlds and played 288 simulated stories, and every world can now be finished.

Made together

Idea, world and playtesting by Francis and family. Code, art, writing and music arrangements by Claude.
